19995-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-05-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for February 1860 is volume 5, number 28. One essay here ponders ancient counting systems. Counting by five fingers and two hands produced the numbers, it argues. Multiplication by five and by two alternately explains the pattern. The Romans adhered to their own mode through it all. Such learned miscellany filled the young magazine's pages. The Atlantic was then barely three years old.

Boston's magazine was already America's literary flagship by 1860. Emerson, Longfellow, and Holmes stood among its founders' circle. Fiction, poetry, science, and review shared each number. February 1860 sits on the edge of a nation about to split. Its calm learning is itself poignant evidence. The issue preserves prewar American intellect at ease.
20033-quin:
Quin appeared in 1921, a novel that opens in the world of dance and wounded men. One man has lain on his back for six months. His legs are still too shaky to hold him well. A friend asks, in sharp words, why he wants to go to a dance at all.

That clash sets the tone for a story about pride, loss, and the wish to live fully again. Talk runs fierce and plain between the men. Readers meet a lead figure who refuses to accept a smaller life. The dance floor becomes a test of will.
20088-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-16-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for November 1865 gathers essays, tales, and verse from leading writers. Volume sixteen, number ninety-seven, came just months after the Civil War ended. One piece weighs beliefs about death across many peoples and faiths. It names Charon and his boat, Dante, and the Muslim hope of paradise.

Monthly issues like this one shaped American thought in the 1860s. Readers of the day found new poems beside grave essays on faith. The issue shows a nation turning from war to deep questions again. It still serves as a window on postwar American letters and belief.
20195-wood-block-printing-a-description-:
F. Morley Fletcher wrote Wood Block Printing, a craft guide based on Japanese practice. Fletcher laments that design was long treated as mere surface looks. Ornament was copied in a mechanical way from an artist's drawing. That artist often knew little of how the work was truly made.

Japanese woodcut craft joins design and making in one skilled hand. Fletcher teaches cutting, inking, and printing step by step for artists. His book helped revive fine woodblock work in the West. Readers get clear craft teaching rooted in respect for the maker's hand.
20203-autobiography-of-benjamin-franklin:
Benjamin Franklin wrote his Autobiography, one of the most read American life stories. This 1916 edition opens with Thomas Jefferson's tale of Franklin at court. Franklin played chess with the old Duchess of Bourbon in France. When he took her king, she said kings are not taken so.

We do in America, Franklin replied, in Jefferson's fond retelling. Inside, Franklin tells of his rise from printer's boy to famed statesman. He shares his plan for moral growth and his shrewd worldly wit. Readers get the classic American tale of self-making, told by its hero.
20232-three-score-years-and-ten-life-lon:
Three Score Years and Ten holds life-long memories of Fort Snelling and the West. One scene recalls a Hartford sitting-room when the century was nineteen. A fair young matron sat beside a cradle in that bright room. In it slept a beautiful boy of a year and a half.

From that tender start, a long life runs west to frontier posts. Fort Snelling stood where rivers meet, at the edge of settlement. Memory books like this one save daily life that histories skip. Readers get seventy years of family, army, and western change in one voice.
20430-the-after-glow-of-a-great-reign-fo:
The After-Glow of a Great Reign collects four addresses given after the death of Queen Victoria. Speakers looked back on her long reign and what it had meant to Britain. The addresses mix praise, mourning, and moral teaching in the manner of sermons.

One speaker takes up a hard question from his text and answers it first. The answer, he says, comes from one who understood human nature, who had sinned and been forgiven. Such turns show how the addresses use scripture and the late queen's example together, to steady a nation in its grief.
20585-sartor-resartus-and-on-heroes-hero:
Thomas Carlyle's Sartor Resartus and On Heroes appear together in this volume, his two most famous works. Sartor Resartus, or The Tailor Retailored, hides a philosophy of life inside a mad German professor's theory of clothes. On Heroes gathers Carlyle's lectures on hero worship through history.

Carlyle loves vast facts. Our theory of gravitation is as good as perfect, he writes. Lagrange has proved the planetary system will endure forever on this scheme, and Laplace guesses it could not have been made on any other. Such sweeps of science serve his real subject: the great souls who steer the world.
20643-the-character-and-influence-of-the:
The Character and Influence of the Indian Trade in Wisconsin is a scholarly study of the fur trade and its effects. It follows the trade from the French era into American hands. Trade goods, posts, and credit bound Native nations and European empires together across the Great Lakes.

The study opens with the broad forces at work. It considers what follows when a higher and a lower civilization meet in commerce, to use its period terms. The Phoenicians, it notes, built trade into a great historic agency, closely tied to piracy at first. Wisconsin's trade is then judged against that long history.
20713-a-campfire-girl-s-first-council-fi:
Jane L. Stewart's A Camp Fire Girl's First Council Fire opens her series about the Camp Fire Girls, the girls' organization founded alongside the Boy Scouts. Its heroine, Bessie, works as a hired girl before the Camp Fire changes her life. The first scenes show her home burden plainly.

There were tears in Bessie's eyes as she went at her dishes. Mrs. Hoover glared at her for a minute, then turned and left the kitchen, muttering about ingratitude. Against that drudgery, the council fire of the title offers friendship, ceremony, and the outdoors. The series sold the new movement to girl readers.
20833-exciting-adventures-of-mister-robe:
Sticks, grass, and mud build Mister Robert Robin's nest in a big basswood fork. Ben Field, in this 1928 tale, hides it so well that none below can spot it. From that safe perch, the robin family's adventures unfold for young readers.

Field wrote nature tales that teach while they charm small children. Robin parents feed, guard, and school their young through the season. Foes, storms, and first flights supply the small thrills. The plain, warm telling suits reading aloud, and its bird lore rests on close watching of real robin life in American yards and woods.
20868-cat-and-dog-or-memoirs-of-puss-and:
Puss the cat looks back on a life of more joy than grief in Cat and Dog. Constant kindness, the cat says, made that happy sum. Memoirs of Puss and the Captain lets two pets tell their own tales.

Mary Martha Sherwood wrote improving tales that mixed fun with moral care. Here, cat and dog recount masters, homes, and scrapes in turn. Animal voices let her teach kindness to beasts by stealth, in warm early children's writing. The tale is told for young readers. Both pets tell their tales in the first person.
20873-albert-gallatin:
No European-born citizen, says this 1883 life, rose higher in American service than Albert Gallatin. His gifts in lawmaking, finance, and diplomacy won praise on both Atlantic shores. Men of science, too, held his name in high regard worldwide.

Henry Adams wrote this compact life of the great Treasury chief. Gallatin funded a young nation, haggled peace at Ghent, and studied native tongues. Adams, himself a sharp historian, keeps the tale lean and keen. The book still serves as a crisp first path into the life of a founder too often left in Jefferson's shade.
21307-fire-island-being-the-adventures-o:
The Planet rides a tremendous sea in the eastern oceans as George Manville Fenn's tale opens. Her crew cling on while Mr Lane advises a life belt. A party of naturalists has shipped aboard her, bound for the island of the title. Their science offers no protection from what waits there.

Chapter after chapter drops the little group and their sailors into fresh danger, with the reader left guessing how each problem can be solved. Fenn was at his best in this mode. Uncertain naturalists face a remote island and perils from sea, weather, beasts, and men, right up to the closing chapters.
21348-benjamin-franklin:
John T. Morse Jr. wrote this life of Benjamin Franklin for the American Statesmen series, published in Boston in 1899. Fifteen chapters run from Franklin's early years through his life as a Philadelphia citizen. They continue through his two missions to England and his years as minister to France. The Hutchinson letters affair and the Privy Council scene get a chapter of their own.

Later chapters cover his financing work and his habits of life and business. The peace talks and his last years at home follow, ending with the Constitutional Convention and his death. Illustrations include Franklin's portrait and Independence Hall. Morse aimed at a compact political life for general readers, in the standard series of its day.
21463-voyages-and-travels-of-count-funni:
Count Funnibos and Baron Stilkin set out to see the world in W. H. G. Kingston's comic tale for the young. The two elderly nobles plan a grand voyage of discovery. In fact, their travels never take them beyond Holland, the land they start from.

Mishaps pile up, the pair part, and chance brings them back together. The Baron vows never to let a problem stop him, however daft his plan. One boot shared between two travellers is a fair sample of the logic. Kingston, rarely comic in his sea tales, here writes pure farce, with many pictures to match.
21654-in-and-around-berlin:
Minerva Brace Norton, an American living abroad, describes Berlin in In and Around Berlin, published in 1889. The approach to the city recalls the newer parts of New York, she writes. There the likeness ends, for Berlin is the heart of a very different nation.

Chapters treat family and social life, education, churches, and museums. The Reichstag and the Prussian Parliament get a chapter, as do famed personages. Norton dedicates the book to her countrymen who have visited Berlin, hope to go, or travel by armchair. Her Berlin is the stiff, bright capital of the young German Empire.
21821-the-mark-of-cain:
A duty dinner at the Olympic Club opens Andrew Lang's novel The Mark of Cain, published in 1886. Maitland of St. Gatien's watches his twenty guests linger over wine and olives, wishing they would go. Even at his own party he feels like an outsider. A strong hand on his shoulder wakes him from his reverie among the scattered fruit.

Lang, known for fairy tales and essays, here tries the modern novel of clubs and society. The title hints at a brand of guilt or fate that a man carries through polite life. Tobacco smoke, cold streets, and close talk fill the opening world. The tale that follows works in Lang's lighter register, curiosity and irony over melodrama.
21842-the-boy-scouts-of-lenox-or-the-hik:
A new scout patrol takes shape in Lenox in this 1915 boys' novel by Frank V. Webster. Tom Chesney, George Cooper, and Carl Oskamp count noses among themselves and find nearly a full patrol. George ought to make a fair scout, his friends allow, even if he is always finding fault. Their big test is the hike over Big Bear Mountain.

The frontispiece shows a rescue, with a boy hoisted to a limb while the next is hauled up. Webster wrote dozens of brisk books for boys, from farm lads to airship pilots. This one rides the first wave of the scouting craze. Woods craft, teamwork, and cheerful grit carry the troop over the mountain and back.
21968-the-finer-grain:
Late tales by Henry James fill The Finer Grain, published in 1910, five stories of success, visits, and quiet desolation. The Velvet Glove opens the book: novelist John Berridge, drunk on his prodigious hit, is sought out in Paris by a young lord. The lord begs the celebrity's judgment on a literary case. Berridge reads the whole scene as one more quaint act on the stage of European society.

A Round of Visits, Crapy Cornelia, and The Bench of Desolation follow in the contents. One tale, Mora Montravers, is missing pages in this text and was removed, as the note explains. James's late style is dense and circling, built for readers who savor motive over event. The finer grain of his title is the grain of feeling itself.
22041-mary-rose-of-mifflin:
Frances R. Sterrett published Mary Rose of Mifflin in 1910. Mary Rose is an orphan, the only child of her aunt's dead sister. When the girl needs a home, her aunt insists on taking her in. Her husband Larry Donovan grumbles at the plan, and the small town of Mifflin watches to see how it will end.

A child who has known little kindness changes the house she enters. Sterrett builds the tale from small scenes, neighbours, and slow softening of hearts. The fight is never about money or villains, only about whether a gruff man can learn to love a child. It is a gentle domestic novel of its period.
22230-hortus-inclusus-messages-from-the-:
John Ruskin wrote Hortus Inclusus as letters to the ladies of the Thwaite at Coniston. The Latin title means "a garden enclosed," and the subtitle calls the pieces messages from the wood to the garden. Ruskin sent them in happy days and dedicated the book to his dear friends in gratitude. They are among the gentlest things the great critic ever wrote.

The letters wander from flowers and woods to womanhood and the names of living creatures. Ruskin finds a small Paradise in a Lake District garden and in the friends who kept it. Late in life his prose here turns soft and grateful. The book is a quiet corner of his vast collected works.
22304-nicanor-teller-of-tales-a-story-of:
Nicanor, Teller of Tales is a story of Roman Britain by C. Bryson Taylor. Even its back matter shows the care behind the tale. A glossary pairs Roman place names with the British places they became.

Readers can match Abus with the Humber River and Tamesis with the Thames. Corinium becomes Cirencester, and Isca Silurum becomes Caerleon. Such a list tells you the fiction rests on a real Roman map. The story brings that occupied Britain to life through its teller, Nicanor. History readers get both a tale and a small gazetteer of Roman Britain in one volume.
22337-history-of-the-moors-of-spain:
History of the Moors of Spain tells how Muslim rulers shaped the Spanish peninsula. The French original had long enjoyed a high reputation. An American lady made the translation offered here.

Her taste and learning, the preface says, well fitted her for the task. Of all Muslim peoples, the Moors of Spain stood renowned in arts and arms. Their story fills the following pages in full. Readers meet a Spain of conquest, courts, and learning. The book also recalls the revival of learning in later medieval centuries. It remains a period account of a civilization that left deep marks on Spain.
22345-memoirs-of-the-private-life-return:
Memoirs of the Private Life, Return, and Reign of Napoleon concerns the emperor in 1815. That was the year of his return from exile and final reign. The writer promises facts that merit close attention from readers.

Study shows a character full of contrasts, the memoir argues. Napoleon appears by turns mistrustful and open, ardent and reserved. He is enterprising yet irresolute, vindictive yet generous. He favors liberty and yet acts the despot. Such a portrait refuses simple praise or blame. Readers get an insider's view of the Hundred Days. It remains useful for anyone tracing how contemporaries judged Napoleon's baffling mix of gifts.
22550-old-mackinaw-or-the-fortress-of-th:
Old Mackinaw, or the Fortress of the Lakes, recounts Michigan's straits country. Mackinac stood guard where Lakes Huron and Michigan meet. Its bibliography alone shows the depth of sources behind the history.

Schoolcraft's works, in three volumes, stand among the chief sources. Shea's Catholic Missions and Discovery of the Mississippi also appear. Lanman's History of Michigan and Parkman's Siege of Pontiac are listed. Foster and Whitney's Geological Report covers the land itself in science. Ferris's Great West and Disturnell's Trip to the Lakes add travel accounts. Readers get a fortress town's story built from many witnesses. French missions, British guns, and American trade all passed that island.
22737-john-gayther-s-garden-and-the-stor:
John Gayther's Garden and the Stories Told Therein is a story collection built around an old gardener and the tales his garden draws out of him; it appeared in 1902. The catalog record names no author. The frame is simple and warm: a garden, its keeper, and the people who pass through it.

John Gayther did not own the garden; he only had charge of it. At busy seasons he had men to help him. For most of the year, though, he preferred to do everything himself. That modest opening sets the book's pace: work, weather, and talk among the beds. Stories told therein grow naturally from the place. Readers who enjoy frame tales and quiet village worlds will find a gentle specimen here.
22874-frank-merriwell-s-pursuit-or-how-t:
Burt L. Standish sends Frank Merriwell into danger in Frank Merriwell's Pursuit, published in 1904. The talk in the excerpt runs hot. Lives hang on the outcome, one man insists. He offers money for aid and asks, practically, whether the house holds any whisky. Merriwell tales rarely pause for breath.

Frank was the clean-living Yale hero of a hugely popular dime-novel series. Each adventure tested his nerve, honesty, and athletic skill against plotters who played dirty. How to Win, the subtitle, states the formula plainly. Modern readers meet here a piece of the reading that shaped American boys a century ago. The values are dated, the pace is not, and the period flavor is the real attraction.
22912-phyllis-a-twin:
Dorothy Whitehill's Phyllis, a Twin, published in 1920, opens in sunshine off Fifth Avenue. In a house a short distance from Central Park, every window stands open. Soft white curtains flutter in a crisp breeze, and cool yellow light floods the rooms. A girls' story could hardly ask for a brighter start.

Phyllis shares her life with a twin, and twinship drives the fun and the mix-ups of this series for young readers. School, friends, and small adventures fill the chapters in the manner of the period's girls' books. Whitehill keeps the tone bright and the stakes friendly. The volume preserves a whole style of wholesome series fiction, written to be passed hand to hand among sisters and friends.
22921-the-death-and-burial-of-cock-robin:
Who'll carry him to his grave, asks The Death and Burial of Cock Robin. The Kite volunteers to bear the body to burial, so long as daylight lasts. The Linnet offers to fetch a torch and carry the light for the procession. So the old rhyme calls its mourners one by one.

Bird after bird takes a part in the burial, the Lark serving as clerk and saying Amen. The verses have taught children rhyme and rhythm for centuries, and picture editions made the procession famous. This printing pairs the familiar questions and answers with illustrations. It is a nursery classic in its simplest form, solemn and playful at once, and built to be read aloud.
23012-elder-conklin:
A girl refuses plainly in Elder Conklin, Frank Harris's story of frontier courtship. Why, just the plainest kind of refusal, I guess, she says. She told the other man only that she felt bound to go with a stranger instead. The refusal, she insists, could not have been plainer. Afraid, she repeats, as if the word stung her. But he'll lose nothing by waiting, nothing. You hear me talk. And her eyes flashed.

The flash promises the story's real subject, a young woman managing rival claims in a raw settlement. Elder Conklin's name carries the respectability she is weighing against a stranger's pull. Harris builds the scene almost wholly from talk, and the talk crackles. His western women rarely wait quietly to be chosen, and this one states her terms herself.
23023-notes-and-queries-number-201-septe:
Notes and Queries, number 201, dated September 3, 1853, trades in literary suspicion. One note quotes a warning about Swinney, a wretched but dangerous fool. He had the impudence, the writer says, to go to Lord G. Sackville, a stranger to him, and ask outright whether he was the author of Junius, the famous anonymous letters. Take care of him, the note ends.

That appetite for attribution fills the whole weekly number. Readers sent questions on books, proverbs, families, and forgotten facts, and other readers answered them. The journal called itself a medium of inter-communication for literary men and artists. Bound runs became a Victorian reference web in print. This single number preserves the correspondence mid-flow, quarrels and all.
328-a-heap-o-livin:
Edgar A. Guest dedicates this little book of verse to Marjorie and Buddy, from their daddy. A Heap o' Livin' opens with When You Know a Fellow, a plea to judge neighbors by their burdens, not their blemishes. Guest's plain rhymes preach kindness and understanding.

Later poems celebrate home, work, friendship, and the daily heap of living. Guest, the people's poet of Detroit, wrote for newspaper readers in simple, warm lines. His verse drew both love and mockery for its sentiment. The book remains a snapshot of homely American optimism.
365-the-land-of-little-rain:
Mary Austin sketches the dry country of eastern California in this set of linked essays. She names the land by its scant rain, then walks its water trails, mesas, and small towns. The Ceriso desert, Shoshone land, Jimville, and the grape-vine town all take their turn in her pages.

Austin watches pocket hunters, basket makers, scavengers, and neighbors with a poet's eye and a neighbor's ear. She gives places Indian names where they fit better than map names. The book endures as a loving, close portrait of desert life, where water rules all and small things matter most.
565-the-zincali-an-account-of-the-gypsie:
George Borrow studies the gypsies of Spain, the Zincali, in this work written over five years on the road. Borrow, distributing scriptures in ventas and posadas, gathered lore on gypsy names, language, law, clans, and fortune-telling. Chapters treat colonies, forges, counts, and the Gitana of Seville.

Borrow writes with vivid, partisan energy, mixing travel, philology, and anecdote. An introduction surveys gypsies from Russia to England. The book endures as a pioneering, if prejudiced, portrait of a people Borrow knew by campfire talk and long road days, not by library alone.
644-the-haunted-man-and-the-ghost-s-barg:
Charles Dickens writes a Christmas ghost tale in this novella, where a learned chemistry teacher is haunted by more than a ghost. The haunted man, hollow-cheeked and grizzled, lives in a chamber part library and part laboratory, where students hang on his lips. A spirit offers him a bargain: to forget his sorrows and lose the power to recall pain.

Dickens writes with rich, somber prose, full of fog, bells, and inner echoes. The gift proves a curse, as a man without memory loses pity too. The tale endures as a lesser-known Christmas book, where Dickens warns that sorrow, rightly borne, keeps the heart human.
698-memoir-of-fleeming-jenkin:
Robert Louis Stevenson wrote this memoir of Fleeming Jenkin, the Scottish engineer and teacher who was his friend. Jenkin worked on telegraph cables, taught at Edinburgh, and wrote on many topics, from drama to trade. Stevenson draws him as a man of restless mind, warm talk, and strong views, liked by students and peers alike.

The memoir first served as an introduction to a set of Jenkin's papers, and it stands alone here. Stevenson blends fact with fond recall, showing Jenkin's work, his home life, and his talk. It gives a vivid portrait of a Victorian man of science who was also a man of letters, seen through the eyes of a novelist who knew him well.
708-the-princess-and-the-goblin:
George MacDonald wrote this fairy tale about Princess Irene, a small girl who lives in a mountain house watched over by her nurse. Below the mountain live goblins, who plot to steal her and marry her to their prince. Curdie, a miner's boy, hears their plans in the mines and warns the household.

Irene finds help from a mysterious great-grandmother, who gives her a thread to follow through dark halls. Courage, trust, and kind deeds guide the children past traps and tunnels. The tale blends wonder with moral weight, and it has long been a favourite first fantasy for young readers.
877-little-britain:
Washington Irving sketched this small London neighbourhood, Little Britain, a cluster of streets in the heart of the great city. He quotes Nashe on the grave ancients within hearing of Bow bell, and he paints a world of old shops, narrow lanes, and neighbours who keep old customs amid new London.

Irving writes with affection for a place that time seems to have passed by, where shopkeepers, clerks, and idlers live by old rules. His sketch is gentle and nostalgic, a piece of local colour from the age of the Sketch Book. It charms readers who love old London, in miniature, before the modern city swept it away.
89-north-american-free-trade-agreement-1:
Trade deals turn on annexes, and this file holds part of one. The North American Free Trade Agreement annex dated October 7, 1992 sets out reservations on investment and services. Each party lists measures that depart from national treatment, most-favored-nation treatment, or local presence rules.

Entries name a sector, sub-sector, industry class, and the obligation concerned. Performance requirements and senior management nationality rules appear alongside. The dry legal form matters: reservations define what the deal does not open. Lawyers and scholars use the annex to read the treaty's true reach.
a-brief-history-of-panics-and-their-peri:
Clément Juglar, a French economist of the Institute, wrote A Brief History of Panics to show that American financial crises return in a pattern, not by chance. The hosted copy is the third edition, translated and edited by DeCourcy W. Thom, who brought the story down from 1889 toward his own day and dated his dedication in October 1915.

Juglar traces crisis after crisis in the United States, comparing prices, credit, speculation, and liquidation as each boom breaks. Thom's additions carry the sequence into the twentieth century, arguing that panic grows from real business conditions, not mere fear. Bankers and students of cycles valued the book because it treated panics as a recurring disease with observable symptoms.
a-heap-o-livin:
Edgar A. Guest collected these homey verses in a little book dedicated to his children, Marjorie and Buddy, as their Daddy. The opening poem, When You Know a Fellow, sets the program: most faults shrink once you know the burdens a man carries. Poem after poem works the same ground in plain rhyme — fathers and children, work and neighbors, grief taken patiently.

Titles such as The Rough Little Rascal show the domestic focus: a small boy with a smudged nose becomes an emblem of what a parent waits all day to meet. Guest wrote for newspaper readers across America, and his verse aims at comfort rather than surprise. The collection preserves the voice of the people's poet at his most characteristic: simple, warm, and certain that home is the center of life.
agobard-de-grandine-et-tonitruis-latin:
Agobard, archbishop of Lyons, wrote his book on hail and thunder around 815, in the age of Charlemagne's heirs. The Latin treatise attacks a belief common among his flock. Farmers held that weather magicians, called tempestarii, raised storms and sold the stolen crops to sky sailors.

Agobard calls the belief folly and proves it from Scripture and reason. He tells of a crowd ready to stone supposed sky travelers, whom he talked down himself. His work is the earliest systematic church attack on folk magic. Theologians quoted him for a thousand years. The Latin text preserves a bishop thinking clearly against the panic of his own parish.
agrippa-de-occulta-philosophia-1533-lati:
Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa published his Three Books of Occult Philosophy in Latin at Cologne in 1533, the first full edition. The work is the foundational synthesis of Renaissance magic. Astrology, Kabbalah, number lore, and natural magic all find their ordered place in Agrippa's vast system.

Book by book, he rises from the elemental world through the celestial to the divine. Every later magus drank from this spring, and most admitted the debt. The Latin text of 1533 is the form in which Europe first read him. Agrippa aimed to restore magic as a learned, pious discipline. His bible of Renaissance magic still anchors any serious study of the occult tradition.
agrippa-de-vanitate-1564-latin:
Agrippa published On the Uncertainty and Vanity of the Sciences in 1530, and this Latin edition of 1564 kept his great skeptical performance in print. The book demolishes the arts and sciences one by one. Grammar, medicine, law, theology, and magic itself all stand accused of vanity and error.

The joke cuts deep, since Agrippa's own Occult Philosophy had taught several of these arts. Readers have debated for centuries how much of the attack he meant. As rhetoric, the De vanitate is a masterpiece of learned doubt. As a companion to the Occult Philosophy, it is unmatched: learn magic first, Agrippa seems to say, then learn to doubt everything, including the lesson.
albumasar-introductorium-1489-latin:
Abu Ma'shar of Baghdad, called Albumasar in Latin, wrote the Great Introduction to astrology in the ninth century. It became the book that taught the Latin West the Arabic system of the art. Hermann of Dalmatia turned it into Latin, and the version here was printed in 1489. No English version in the public domain exists.

Albumasar grounds the power of the stars in physics, sorting signs, planets, houses, and aspects into one great scheme. Kings and scholars across Europe used his book to read the heavens for three centuries. The printed Latin of 1489 shows the work at the height of its fame. It stands as the record of how Arabic astrology remade a science in the West.
alcabitius-isagoge-1521-latin:
Al-Qabisi, a scholar of Aleppo in the tenth century, wrote the Isagoge as a short first book for students of astrology. For the rest of the Middle Ages it served as the standard beginner's text in the Latin West. The edition here is the Latin printing from Venice in 1521, with the commentary of John of Saxony.

Five chapters lay out the signs, the planets, the houses, and the terms a judge of the stars must know. John of Saxony, a Paris master of the 1300s, explains each point for the classroom. No English version in the public domain exists. The little book shows how a whole science was taught, one clear rule at a time.
allan-quatermain:
H. Rider Haggard sent his hunter hero Allan Quatermain on his last trek in this book of 1887. It is the mate to King Solomon's Mines, the hit of two years past. Haggard wrote it while the fame of the first book was still fresh and high.

Quatermain, now old, joins a last hunt for a lost white race in the heart of Africa. Strange priests, a vast cave world, and a doom that hangs on the band fill the tale. The book turns the brisk hunter of the first tale into a figure of myth.
an-inquiry-into-the-nature-and-progress-:
Thomas Robert Malthus published his Inquiry into the Nature and Progress of Rent in London in 1815. Malthus, a clergyman and professor at the East India College, drew the tract from his lecture notes. Its subject is rent, the share of farm produce that stays with the landowner. The argument speaks directly to the corn law debates of that year.

Malthus defines rent by what remains after the costs of cultivation and ordinary farm profits are paid. He asks why raw produce sells at a high price and disputes the answers of Adam Smith and the French Economists. Rent, he argues, is no mere monopoly gain but grows from fertile soil and rising demand. The pamphlet helped shape classical economics and the case over grain imports.
annals-and-reminiscences-of-jamaica-plai:
Harriet Manning Whitcomb explains the making of her sketch. She prepared it to be read before the Jamaica Plain Ladies' Tuesday Club. She then printed it at her friends' wish. She sold it at a fair for the Jamaica Plain Indian Association. She drew on the Memorial History of Boston, Drake's Town of Roxbury, and the memory of older residents, and she begs indulgent criticism for any errors. The imprint is Cambridge, 1897.

Her annals follow Jamaica Plain, once part of Roxbury and now a Boston neighborhood, through its farms, ponds, great houses, churches, and the families who held them. Reminiscence mixes with record: who lived where, what stood before the streetcars came. Local history of this kind preserves what no larger history bothers to keep.
arse-ne-lupin:
Arsène Lupin, the English novel credited on its title page to Edgar Jepson and Maurice Leblanc, brings France's gentleman thief to the château of the Dukes of Charmerace. A millionaire's daughter writes among her family's treasures as the story opens. The Duke of Charmerace arrives, motor-cars vanish, and a letter from Lupin announces more thefts to come. Detective Guerchard opens the inquiry, with secretary Sonia caught between suspicion and loyalty.

Inside, pendant, cars, and telephone wires disappear or fail in a duel of wits across twenty-three chapters. Lupin moves through the house in plain sight, since disguise is his native country. Guerchard picks up the true scent only to find his quarry bargaining from strength. Readers get the Lupin formula in early, polished form: crime as sport, the police a move behind, and a thief whose charm is meant to make honesty look slow.
augustine-de-divinatione-daemonum-latin:
Augustine of Hippo wrote De divinatione daemonum, on the divination of demons, around 413. The short Latin treatise asks a sharp question. If demons foretell the future truly, as pagans claimed, why must Christians refuse their oracles?

Augustine answers that demons guess shrewdly rather than know. Keen senses, long memory, and swift travel let them predict much, he argues. Their hits prove no divine gift, and their aim is to trap human souls. The treatise became foundational for all medieval demonology. Later writers on witchcraft built on Augustine's frame. Here it stands in its original Latin, brief and decisive.
bacon-epistola-secretis-1618-latin:
Roger Bacon, the thirteenth-century Franciscan, addressed his Letter on the Secret Works of Art and Nature to a learned reader of his day. John Dee edited this Latin printing of 1618, a fitting match of editor and author. The epistle ranges over marvels, magic, and natural philosophy in Bacon's bold voice.

Bacon describes wonders that art and nature can work without demons. Flying machines, great ships, and burning mirrors pass in review as things knowledge might achieve. He writes like a prophet of experimental science. Dee, who owned more Bacon manuscripts than anyone, gave the letter to the press. Readers meet the medieval friar whom later ages turned into a magician, arguing here for nature's hidden powers.
brentano-das-marchen-von-dem-myrtenfraul:
Clemens Brentano wove Italian folk material into his fairy tale of the myrtle maiden, Das Maerchen von dem Myrtenfraeulein, given here in German. A plant, a maiden, and a secret life hidden inside green leaves carry the story. Brentano was the most musical of the German Romantics, and his tales sing on the page.

Love and transformation govern the plot, as folk wonders receive a poet's lush retelling. The marvelous feels natural in Brentano's hands, which is the fairy tale's oldest trick done perfectly. Readers of German will hear his verbal music at full strength. The tale shows why his name anchors the Romantic fairy tale. Small in size, the piece holds a whole enchanted garden inside it.
bruno-de-magia-latin:
Giordano Bruno wrote De Magia, on magic, in Latin near the end of his wandering life, around 1590. Bruno treats magic as the art of bonds. All things, he argues, are linked by attractions and sympathies, and the magus works by knowing and pulling those links.

 His system sorts magic into kinds and traces how images, words, and desires bind souls. The treatise is the philosophical peak of Renaissance magic theory. Bruno the thinker of infinite worlds stands behind every page. Burned at Rome in 1600, he left this calm, daring account of his art. Readers meet the mind for which the cosmos itself was the great web of bonds.
c-f-meyer-die-richterin:
A woman holds the power of justice in Charlemagne's age and must judge her own family's crimes. C. F. Meyer's Die Richterin, given here in German, builds its tragedy around Stemma, the judge of its title. Few heroines in German fiction carry her sternness and sorrow in equal measure.

Guilt and atonement govern the plot, as hidden sins surface under her own tribunal. Meyer writes the early medieval world with his usual lapidary force, every scene cut clean. Stemma's strength is real, and so is the price it exacts from her heart. Critics call the novella the master's late masterpiece. Magnificently written, it closes his career on a note of stern, tragic grandeur.
canon-episcopi-latin:
The Canon Episcopi is a church law text from around 900, passed down through Regino of Prüm's collection. It treats the belief that certain women ride at night with Diana or Herodias. The canon declares the night flight an illusion worked by demons, not a bodily fact.

That ruling mattered for centuries. Canon lawyers quoted the text for six hundred years, and it long held back full-blown witch persecution. Later demonologists had to argue around its plain denial. The canon shows the early medieval church as the skeptic in the room. Its Latin lines are brief, but few texts on witchcraft have been cited more often or fought over harder.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-lehn: The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Lehnin describes a Cistercian abbey founded in 1180 by Otto the Second, Margrave of Brandenburg. It stood about eight miles south-east of Brandenburg, and its church showed fine Romanesque building. Lehnin matters chiefly for the famous Vaticinium Lehninense, a prophecy supposedly penned by a monk called Hermann in the 1200s or 1300s. First printed in 1722, it laments the Ascanian line's end in 1319, portrays later margraves, and ends the Hohenzollern house with Frederick William the Third.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abthain:
Abthain, or abthane, is the English or Lowland Scotch shape of middle-Latin abthania, from Gaelic abdhaine, meaning abbacy. The word's exact sense was lost, so people took it to denote some ancient dignity, whose holder went by abthanus or abthane. Dr. Skene holds that the correct meaning is abbey or monastery, not abbot or over-thane.

The word refers chiefly to territories of churches and monasteries founded by old Celtic or Columban monks, chiefly from the Mounth range to the Firth of Forth. Many of these abthains passed into lay hands, descending from father to son. They paid certain church tributes and matched the early Irish church's termon lands closely. Skene recommends the forms abthany or abthanry.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adele-amalie-:
Adele Amalie Gallitzin, or Golyzin, was a princess born at Berlin on 28 August 1748. She died at Angelmodde near Munster on 17 April 1806. Daughter of Prussia's General Count von Schmettau, she was educated Catholic but soon grew estranged from religion. In 1768 she married Russia's Prince Dimitry Gallitzin, ambassador under Catherine II at Paris, Turin, and The Hague.

There her beauty and qualities of mind and heart won her a brilliant role. At twenty-four she suddenly left society and devoted herself to her children's education. She studied mathematics, classical philology, and philosophy under Franz Hemsterhuis, who kindled her Socratic-Platonic enthusiasm. Drawn to Munster by Furstenberg's educational reform, she became centre of an intellectual circle including Overberg, Droste-Vischering, Stolberg, and Hamann. She later returned to the church, and her gentle charity blessed many.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-akhmin:
Akhmin is a city of Upper Egypt on the Nile's banks. Of late years it has gained great importance from discoveries in its cemeteries. Akhmin's hill, some two miles long, is filled with remains piled in pits of eight or ten small chambers, a dozen coffins in each.

Heathens and Christians lie heaped together, so often one cannot say whether a body's little articles belonged to a heathen, a Christian, or a sect member. Eutychianism had become almost the whole Coptic nation's religion from the fifth century onward. Papyri and tapestries chiefly famed the city. Among the papyri, the Gospel of Peter, Apocalypse of Peter, and Book of Henoch fragments hold first place. The tapestries have supplied first-rank material for ancient textile handicrafts' history, in excellent preservation and great variety.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-albert-jean-b:
Albert Jean Belin was a French prelate, a senior churchman, and writer. He was born at Besançon early in the seventeenth century and died in April 1677. He entered the Benedictine monastery of Faverney in 1629 and later served as prior and abbot at houses including Charité-sur-Loire, Nevers, and Paris. He was consecrated Bishop of Belley in February 1666.

Belin wrote in French, and his books ranged from works on the philosopher's stone and talismans to proofs of Christian truth and eucharistic emblems, many dated 1653. The entry notes he is probably the same man as Alphonsus Belin, prior of Charité-sur-Loire, author of a 1683 defence of Catholic teaching against the Reformed faith.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-albrecht-von-:
Albrecht von Wallenstein, also called Waldstein, was an imperial general, born in Bohemia in September 1583 and dead at Eger in February 1634. He came from a Czech noble family of the Bohemian Brethren and studied at the Lutheran university of Altdorf. He travelled in France and Italy and turned Catholic, apparently at the Jesuit college of Olmütz. An elderly widow's fortune, inherited in 1614, launched his rise.

Wallenstein first commanded independently in 1621 against Bethlen Gabor in Moravia. After lending Ferdinand large sums, he gained confiscated Bohemian estates that became the principality of Friedland in 1624. In April 1625 Ferdinand made him captain over all imperial forces, and he raised an army of 20,000 men. Later campaigns drove Mansfeld from Silesia and carried him to Jutland and Mecklenburg. The entry judges his standing as a general disputed and his later life a tangle of intrigue ending in treason.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alcuin:
Alcuin, also called Alhwin or Flaccus, was an eminent teacher, scholar, and theologian, born about 735 of noble Northumbrian parentage and dead on 19 May 804. His birthplace is disputed, though it was probably in or near York. As a child he entered the cathedral school founded there by Archbishop Egbert. When his master Aelbert became archbishop in 767, the direction of the school fell to Alcuin.

Alcuin had the largest share in the revival of learning of his age, the entry says. He worked as a teacher and gatherer of knowledge rather than an originator. His work reached beyond York to the Palace School, part of Charlemagne's broad plans for spreading learning. As a theologian he wrote on Scripture, morals, and doctrine, standing as the Church's foremost champion against the Adoptionist heresy. As a liturgist he was the chief agent of the reform of worship carried out under Charlemagne's authority.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-curtain:
Altar curtains once hung between the columns of the ciborium, the cupola over the high altar in most basilicas, cathedrals, and large churches. Metal rods held rings fastening curtains, called tetravela altaris, of linen, silk, gold cloth, and other precious stuffs, drawn around the altar at set parts of Mass. Roman pontiffs such as Gregory IV, Leo IV, and Nicholas I gave such curtains to Rome's churches.

When ciboria fell out of use, a dossel or dorsal hung at the altar's back, with two more at its sides, on wall rods, reredos rods, or four pillars. Angels holding candelabra crowned the pillars, candles burning there on solemn occasions. Today's sanctuary candelabra probably descend from these pillar lights.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andre-garin:
Andre Garin, an Oblate missionary priest, was born in 1822 at Cote-Saint-Andre, Isere, and died at Lowell, Massachusetts, in 1895. He studied at his native town's lesser seminary and entered the Oblates of Mary Immaculate on 1 November 1842. Too young for the priesthood, he went to Canada and was ordained in 1845 by Bishop Bourget of Montreal.

For twelve years he served eastern Canada's Indian missions, then served as superior at Plattsburg and Buffalo. His mastery of Montagnais and English aided his early work. When Lowell needed an able man to organize its French Canadians, Garin was ordered there. His good sense, courteous manner, and kindly temper soon won him wonderful influence over his people. During some twenty-five years as pastor he built costly churches and commodious schools and founded several religious confraternities. Two years after his death his parishioners raised a statue to him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anne-therese-:
Anne-Thérèse Guérin, Mother Theodore in religion, born at Etables in 1798, died in 1856. She entered the Sisters of Providence in 1823, professed vows in 1824, and became Rennes superior the same day. Transferred to Soulaines in 1833, she founded St. Mary-of-the-Woods, Indiana, in 1840, and became superior general in America.

The Life and Life-Work of 1904 calls her a woman of uncommon valour. Father Charles Coppens adds that she was superior in gifts and virtues, living in union with God, practising heroic faith, hope, and charity. A model of virtue for the faithful, especially religious men and women. Her mind was superior: the French Academy gave her medallions, she was skilled in medicine and theology, and her institution's expansion evidences her energetic spirit.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-artvin:
Artvin, a Russian city in the Transcaucasian province of Kutais, stands beside Turkish Armenia on the left bank of Tehoruk, which flows to the Black Sea. By 1894 it held 5,900 people, mostly Armenian and Turkish. In Artvin and its vicinity stood nine Armenian-Catholic churches, four boys' schools and three for girls, while Gregorian Armenians held five churches and two schoolhouses.

The Armenian-Catholic diocese of Artvin was set up in 1850 by Pius IX for United Armenians in southern Russia. It was first suffragan to Constantinople's metropolitan, then answerable to the Armenian-Catholic Cilician patriarch, whose see is Constantinople. Its first bishop, Timotheus Astorgi, served from 1850 to 1858, followed by Antonius Halagi in 1859 and Joannes Baptista Zaccharian in 1878. That year Russia annexed the whole diocese and joined it to Tiraspol, blocking later bishops.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ascelin:
Ascelin, ambassador of Innocent IV, pope from 1243 to 1254, to the Tartars, entered the Dominican order, likely at Paris, in 1221 or 1222. Distinguished for learning and great zeal for spreading Christian faith, he was chosen in 1245 with three fellow Dominicans by Humbert de Romanis, provincial of France. The pope had ordered Humbert to pick fit men for an embassy to convert Sultan Melik Saleh, then camped in Persia.

On Vincent of Beauvais's authority, drawn from embassy member Simon of St. Quentin, they met the sultan's first great army on 24 May 1247. Their mission failed, since they brought no presents to win mercenary courtiers, and Ascelin refused to kneel three times in honour of the khan's dignity. Condemned to death, the friars faced the khan's threat to flay their leader Ascelin, and the entry follows a mission undone by protocol and pride.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-august-allers:
August Allerstein, also called Hallerstein, was a Jesuit missionary in China who died there probably about 1777, after the suppression of his order. His skill in mathematics and astronomy won him favor at the imperial court in Peking. Emperor Kiang-long raised him to mandarin rank and put him in charge of the Department of Mathematics, where he stayed for many years. The court post gave him access to figures few Europeans could obtain.

His lasting gift to Europe was a census of China for the twenty-fifth and twenty-sixth years of Kiang-long's reign, reaching the West in 1779. The work mattered because the Tatar rulers disliked census-taking, fearing the Chinese might grasp their own strength and grow restless. It also confirmed the reckonings of his predecessor Father Amiot. It showed a rising population, with 196,837,977 souls counted in the first year and 198,214,624 in the next.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-augustus-welb:
Augustus Welby Northmore Pugin was an English architect and archaeologist born in London in 1812, who died at Ramsgate in 1852. He was the only child of Augustus Charles Pugin, a French Protestant draughtsman who had fled France for London. The boy learned drawing from his father, inheriting his delicacy and dexterity, and force of character and piety from his mother. At fourteen he prepared drawings of Rochester Castle. The next year he sketched in Notre Dame in Paris while suffering from overwork.

In youth he designed furniture for Windsor Castle, built a model stage at home, made scenery for Kenilworth, and rearranged Drury Lane's stage machinery. A passion for the sea gave him his own smack, a small sailing boat. His creed was the Gothic embodiment of art as the only true Christian architecture. His merit, it says, was restoring architecture in England and reviving medieval forms across the land.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-baldwin:
Baldwin was Archbishop of Trier and Elector of the Holy Roman Empire, born in 1285, who died in 1354. He belonged to Luxemburg's noble counts and was brother to Emperor Henry VII. His father died in battle when Baldwin was three, so his mother Beatrix and his brother schooled him. At thirteen he went to Paris University under two private tutors and gained a thorough education.

In 1305 Henry sought Mainz for his nineteen-year-old brother, but Clement V refused so great a see to a youth. When Aichspalter cured the pope's severe sickness, he won Mainz himself, with Baldwin to follow Diether at Trier. Diether died in 1307, and Baldwin, consecrated at Poitiers in March 1308, took Trier that June. Aged only twenty-two, he filled the triple office of bishop, prince, and elector, paying old debts without new taxes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bassein:
Bassein is a town twenty-nine miles north of Bombay, a historic old Portuguese settlement in India. St Gonsalo Garcia, the only Indian saint, was born here, later crucified with Japan's first martyrs at Nagasaki in 1597. Founded in 1536 by Nunho de Cunha, who took the island from Bahadur Shali of Gujerat, it became Portugal's chief northern Indian settlement.

Rich timber, fertility, and a healthy climate made it a commercial center and home to many Portuguese noblemen. Franciscan Antonio do Porto, the Apostle of Bassein, is credited with converting 10,156 pagans. Mahrattas took it in 1739 and the English in 1802, leaving a ruined town whose fort ranks among India's finest Portuguese ruins. It remains a Christian oasis with nine churches, twelve priests, and 16,119 Catholics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-benin:
Benin, the Vicariate Apostolic of the Coast of Benin, is a mission entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. It covers a wide stretch of Upper Guinea on the Gulf of Guinea, once part of a great West African kingdom. A mission founded in Dahomey in 1860 took the Benin name because local people disliked the Dahomey title.

Splits soon shrank the vicariate, with Dahomey cut off in 1882 and the Niger mission in 1894. What remained lay between Dahomey, the Niger country, and the sea. The entry lists stations, clergy, schools, and converts, giving a working report on a young African mission at the century's turn.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-benjamin:
Benjamin, the youngest son of Jacob, receives a scriptural entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. His Hebrew name means son of the right hand, though his dying mother Rachel first called him Ben-oni, son of my sorrow, and Jacob changed it. After Joseph's loss, Jacob lavished affection on Benjamin, his last link to Rachel.

Reluctance marks the story: Jacob only let Benjamin travel to Egypt for corn under pressure, and Joseph showed him marked favour there. The entry then follows the tribe of Benjamin, its land, its warriors, and its later place in Israel's history. It joins a family tale to a tribal history in one compact piece.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-berlin:
Berlin, capital of the German Empire and of Prussia, receives a substantial entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. The city, on the Spree in Brandenburg, held just over two million people in 1905, of whom about 224,000 were Catholics. It grew from two Wendish settlements, Kölln on a Spree island and Berlin across the water.

History dominates the piece, from medieval revolts against Hohenzollern electors to the castle that became the royal residence. Later sections cover Catholic parishes, schools, hospitals, and orders in a largely Protestant capital. The entry joins civic history to a census of Catholic life in imperial Berlin.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bernard-dorni:
Bernard Dornin, the first American publisher of books distinctly Catholic in character, is the subject of this short 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born in Ireland in 1761, he died in Ohio in 1836 after political trouble drove him from home in 1803. Arriving in New York, he opened a book-selling and publishing business.

A New Testament printed in Brooklyn in 1805 and Pastorini's History of the Church in 1807 began his list. Moves to Baltimore in 1809 and Philadelphia in 1817 kept him at the head of American Catholic publishing for years. Archbishop Carroll and other bishops prized him as a vigorous writer and a trusted friend of the hierarchy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-frowin:
Blessed Frowin, Benedictine abbot of Engelberg, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Nothing is known of his early life, save that historians of both Einsiedeln and St. Blasius claim him as their monk. His first sure fact is election as abbot of Engelberg in 1142, succeeding St. Adelhelm in the newly founded Swiss house.

As abbot he stood out for holiness, learning, and able rule, greatly enlarging the abbey's lands and privileges, civil and church alike. Its fame for study grew under him. He died in 1178, leaving Engelberg a strong and honoured monastery. The entry presents an abbot known mainly by his works.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-ralph-sher:
Blessed Ralph Sherwin, an English martyr, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born in 1550 at Rodesley near Longford in Derbyshire, he died at Tyburn in 1581. Nominated by Sir William Petre to a fellowship at Exeter College, Oxford, he took his M.A. in 1574, famed as an acute philosopher and a fine Greek and Hebrew scholar.

Fleeing abroad in 1575, he was ordained at Douai in 1577 and returned to England's mission. Arrested and racked in the Tower, he was tried for treason as a priest and executed with Edmund Campion's companions. The entry presents a scholar-priest among the first Douai martyrs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cain:
Cain, the first-born of Adam and Eve, took his name from the Hebrew root kanah, to possess, recalling his mother's words at his birth. Genesis casts him as a tiller of the soil while his brother Abel kept flocks, and both offered sacrifice to God. Cain gave fruits of the earth, Abel the firstlings of his flock, and God accepted Abel's offering while rejecting Cain's, for reasons the text leaves unstated.

Commentators long debated the cause. One view, from the Septuagint, holds that Cain offered well but divided badly, keeping the better share for himself. Saint Augustine held that Cain gave God goods but not his heart. Angered by the rejection, Cain killed Abel, and Saint John ascribes the murder to Cain's evil works set against his brother's just ones.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cartagena-spa:
Cartagena in Spain is a diocese suffragan to Granada since the concordat of 1851, and before that to Toledo. It covers Murcia and Albacete with towns in Alicante and Almeria, and its bishop lives at Murcia, a city of 111,539 people. Vandals nearly destroyed Cartagena in 425, and some writers infer it then lost metropolitan rank, though a Bishop Hector signed the decrees of Tarragona in 516.

Byzantines rebuilt the city. Bishop Licinianus wrote theological epistles late in the sixth century. After the Byzantine expulsion in 674 the see lapsed, with a Bishop John recorded under Moorish rule in 998. The city returned to Christian hands in 1247, and the see was restored under the Franciscan Pedro Gallego, confessor of Alfonso X. Nicholas IV moved the bishop's residence to Murcia in 1291 to escape pirate raids. Later bishops include Siliceo, tutor of Philip II, and Cardinal Belluga.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chaplain:
Chaplain comes from Latin capellanus, from capella, chapel. The favored derivation, drawn by Du Cange from earlier writers, traces capella to St. Martin of Tours' capa or capella, a short cloak the kings of France kept as a relic. Carried into war and enshrined under a tent on the field, the relic gave the tent the name capella, and its custodians became the capellani.

Others hold that capella simply means a covering. They say the name came from the tent-like structure French kings raised over the altar for soldiers in the field, with no link to St. Martin's relic. If the St. Martin derivation is right, court chaplains began as the clerics guarding sacred relics in royal palaces. In time they gained leave to say Mass in the oratories under their care, with spiritual jurisdiction over palace residents. They became confessors and teachers of all frequenting the court chapel.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-dumou:
Charles Dumoulin was a French jurist born at Paris in 1500 and dead there in 1566. He came of a noble family related to Anne Boleyn, mother of Elizabeth of England. After his doctorate in law he lectured at Orléans in 1521 and became an advocate of the Parlement of Paris. He soon left that post to study law alone, winning a great reputation for jurisprudence.

In 1542 he embraced Calvinism, then soon passed to Lutheranism, and violent attacks on the papacy forced him to seek refuge in Germany. He lectured on law at Tübingen in 1553 and afterwards at Strasburg, Dôle, and Besançon. Back in Paris in 1557, he was soon forced out again to Orléans and Lyons, returning to Paris in 1564. On his deathbed he renounced his errors and made peace with the Church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-franc:
Charles-Francois Toustain was a French Benedictine of the Congregation of St-Maur, born at Repas in 1700 and dead at St-Denis in 1754. He came of a family of note and made his vows at Jumièges in 1718. After philosophy and theology at Fécamp, he went to Bonne-Nouvelle at Rouen to learn Hebrew and Greek. Ordained priest only in 1729, he approached Mass nervously and only after long preparation.

In 1730 he entered St-Ouen, later moving to St-Germain-des-Près and Blancs-Manteaux, and died while taking a milk cure at St-Denis. Fasts and ascetic practices had worn out his body. For twenty years he worked with his fellow monk Tassin on an edition of St. Theodore of Studium that never found a publisher. Their joint Nouveau traité de diplomatique, in six volumes from 1750 to 1765, treated its subject more fully and thoroughly than before.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-josep:
A biographical entry on Charles Joseph de Harlez, a Belgian priest and scholar of the ancient East who taught at Louvain. Born at Liège in 1832 to an old noble family, he first studied law with distinction, then abandoned a promising legal career for theology and ordination in 1858. After teaching posts at Huy and Louvain, he took up the chair of Oriental studies in 1871.

De Harlez poured his energy into the Zend-Avesta, the sacred writings of Zoroastrianism, a religion founded by the prophet Zoroaster. His French translation of 1875 to 1877, revised in 1881, advanced study of the text and of Old Persian language. He also argued that the Avesta and the Rig-Veda, the early hymns of India, differ more deeply than they seem to agree, a view his critics came to accept.

A short life of Charles Joseph Tricassin, a seventeenth-century Capuchin theologian from Troyes who died in 1681. Little is known of his personal history. The entry presents him as a deep student of Augustine, the early Church father whose teaching on grace shaped Catholic debate for centuries. Tricassin defended Augustine's doctrine against the Jansenists, a movement that stressed human helplessness without grace.

His books take up predestination, the belief that God destines some people for glory, the freedom of the fallen will, and grace sufficient for every person. They include Latin treatises printed at Paris between 1669 and 1679, a commentary on Augustine, and a French version of Augustine on grace and free will. His opponents, unable to answer him, reportedly bought up his books and burned them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-louis:
An entry on Charles de la Vallée Poussin, the Belgian geologist who created the teaching of geology and mineralogy at Louvain. Born at Namur in 1827, he studied humanities there and mathematics in Paris, spending ten years on literature and philosophy before turning to science. Appointed professor in 1863 on Omalius d'Halloy's recommendation, he built the university's courses in geology, the study of the earth, and mineralogy, the study of minerals, from scratch.

His papers, scattered through journals from 1876 to 1903, put him among the foremost Belgian geologists and crystallographers, students of crystal structure. Memoirs with A. F. Renard on the microscopic study of crystalline rocks won a Royal Academy prize and became a classic. He also fixed the true layering of Belgian coal-bearing limestone, studied how the Meuse valley formed, and helped prepare the official geological map of Belgium before his death at Brussels in 1903.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-rolli:
A life of Charles Rollin, the French educator and historian who wrote his famous books only in retirement. Born in Paris in 1661, the son of a cutler, he won a college scholarship through his piety, studied theology, and taught rhetoric at the Collège de Plessis. At thirty-three he became rector of the university, and in 1696 principal of the Collège de Beauvais, dismissed in 1722 for opposing the papal bull Unigenitus.

Rollin began his Traité des Études, a guide to teaching literature, near the age of sixty. It urged studying national history and schoolbooks in the everyday language. His Ancient History ran to twelve volumes, and his Roman History, left unfinished at his death in 1741, shows warmth and ease but little critical bite. The entry also notes his share in the Jansenist St. Médard cemetery scenes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christophe-pl:
An entry on Christophe Plantin, bookbinder and publisher of Antwerp, born near Tours in 1514. The son of a servant, he learned binding and printing at Caen from 1535 to 1540, knew Latin early, and loved scientific books. After a short stay in Paris he reached Antwerp in 1548 and opened a bindery famed for inlaid bindings. In 1555 he founded a publishing house that within five years ranked first among typographers of his time.

Charged in 1562 with dealing with two religious reformers, Plantin fled Antwerp, then cleared himself. Only after two centuries did his Familist links and his printing of heretical works come to light. His great feat was the Biblia Regia, the eight-volume royal polyglot Bible finished in 1573 with Philip the Second's backing. The king then made him Royal Architypographer for breviaries, missals, and psalters, a privilege his successors held for two hundred years.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-church-latin:
An entry on church Latin, the Latin of the Church's official books, the Bible and the liturgy, and of Western Christian writers expounding or defending the faith. It differs from classical Latin chiefly by new idioms and new words, while in syntax and literary method Christian writers match their contemporaries. Those differences come from the origin and purpose of church Latin itself.

Early Rome spoke prisca latinitas, the old tongue of Latium, until Ennius and others, trained by Greeks, enriched it for cultured circles. That polished idiom became classical Latin, preserved purest in Caesar and Cicero, while the populace kept the old speech, the sermo vulgaris. Daily contact forced cultured writers to borrow vulgar words, producing a mixed everyday idiom, the sermo cotidianus. From that living speech, shaped by Scripture and worship, church Latin grew.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-claude-de-lor:
Claude de Lorrain, a French painter and etcher, was born in 1600 at Chamagne on the Moselle and died at Rome in November 1681 or 1682. He grew up poor in a large family and was orphaned by twelve. He lived with a wood-carver elder brother at Freiburg, learning to draw ornaments and arabesques. Sandrart says he was apprenticed to a pastry-cook, though pistori may misprint pictori, painter. About 1613 a relative took him to Rome and abandoned him.

He sought Gottfried Wals at Naples, who taught him perspective and landscape. Back in Rome in 1615, he joined Agostino Tassi's household as half servant, half assistant. After Venice in 1625, a Loreto pilgrimage, and wanderings through Tyrol, Bavaria, the Black Forest, and Nancy, he settled in Rome in 1627 for life. Popes, Emperor Leopold the First, and Philip the Fourth of Spain commissioned him, and in 1644 alone he finished seventeen important canvases.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cochin:
Cochin, on India's Malabar coast, became suffragan to Goa by Paul the Fourth's bull of 4 February 1558. Leo the Thirteenth reorganised it under the Concordat of 23 June 1886 and the constitution Humanae Salutis Auctor of 1 September 1886, leaving it suffragan to Goa. The diocese forms two coastal strips, the first about fifty miles long and eight at its broadest, the second thirty miles long. Its higher institutions stand at Cochin and Alleppi.

When the Portuguese arrived, Malabar professed Hinduism, the Christianity of Saint Thomas, Islam, and Judaism, the last in a large colony. The Catholic community drew mostly from Nestorians and Hindus, with a fair share from Islam and rare converts among Jews. Portugal began Catholic mission work in India, and Cochin claims honour as its cradle. Eight Franciscan friars sailed from Lisbon with Cabral in 1500. Three were slain at Calicut on 16 November 1500, and the survivors reached Cochin about 26 November.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-comte-de-la-r:
Pierre Marique's entry follows the Comte de La Rochejacquelein, French politician born at Citran on 28 September 1805, dead on 7 January 1867. His old family name runs back to Saint Louis's Crusade of 1248. His father Louis and uncle Henri won fame as royalist generals in the Vendée wars. His mother left much-edited memoirs. At sixteen he entered Saint-Cyr, won a cavalry commission in 1823, and fought in Spain and the Russo-Turkish War of 1828.

Made a peer in 1825, he resigned after the Revolution of 1830 brought younger Bourbons to the throne. Morbihan sent him to the legislature in 1842, where he sat with the Legitimist Right, sometimes backing liberal measures. In 1848 the Gazette de France backed his presidential candidacy, with few votes. Napoleon III made him senator in 1852, to Legitimist surprise. In the senate he defended Catholicism, though Marique faults his imperial foreign policy backing. He published works on taxes, pensions, and France.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-convent-schoo:
George Cyprian Alston's entry treats convent education in Great Britain. Educating the young ranks nearly as old as religious life for women. From earliest times English children learned in convents. Eighth-century Wimborne nuns, helping Saint Boniface evangelize Saxony, founded convent schools wherever they went, reaching high scholarship. Medieval writers show English convent schools comparing favourably with boys' schools. All this ended at the Reformation in England.

Numerous convents opening in later nineteenth-century England produced numerous convent schools. Secondary schools stand almost all under Government inspection, with wide studies and fully qualified teachers. Over two hundred Catholic secondary schools in England serve under about sixty orders. Only Catholic students had been admitted hitherto, but September 1908 Board regulations changed admission. Higher education for women through convents barely leaves experiment. Ireland's and Scotland's convent schools compare favourably with England's. Superiors of England's principal teaching orders supplied most information.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-count-leo-thu:
A biographical entry traces Count Leo Thun-Hohenstein, an Austrian statesman born in Bohemia in 1811 and dead in Vienna in 1888, whose career linked prison reform, Czech culture, and imperial politics. Educated at Prague in law and philosophy, he studied England's political system and, in Paris, its prisons and charities for working people.

His first publication urged moral reform of prisons, and a later treatise defended Czech language and literature. During the 1848 revolution he became the effective ruler of Bohemia, was captured by insurgents at Prague, and later served as minister of education and religion. In later life he led Bohemia's Federalist party, defending full autonomy for the kingdom, and founded its newspaper, the Vaterland.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-demetrius-aug:
A biographical entry follows Demetrius Augustine Gallitzin, born at The Hague in 1770 and dead at Loretto, Pennsylvania, in 1840, who lived as prince, priest, and missionary. He came of one of Russia's oldest and richest families. His father had served fourteen years as ambassador to France, moving among Diderot, Voltaire, and d'Alembert. He professed godless philosophy despite nominal Orthodoxy.

His mother Amalie, baptized Catholic but religiously neglected, became fervent in 1786, and young Demetrius, baptized Orthodox and strictly disciplined, became a sincere Catholic near seventeen. Ordained for America, he reached Pennsylvania in 1792 and laboured forty years in the Alleghenies. At Loretto he built church and community, wrote books in defence of the Faith, and became known as the Apostle of the Alleghenies, dying amid the flock he had served. He gave his life to a rough frontier flock, riding long miles to sick beds and far farms.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-denis-lambin:
A life of Denis Lambin, a French scholar of Greek and Latin born about 1520 at Montreuil-sur-mer, who died at Paris in 1572. Service with Cardinal de Tournon took him twice to Italy, where he met leading Italian scholars and began translating Aristotle. Shock at the Massacre of Saint Bartholomew is said to have hastened his death.

At the Collège de France he held the Latin chair, then moved to Greek, while his editions of Horace, Lucretius, Cicero, and Nepos opened a new era in their texts. His translations also covered Aristotle's Ethics and Politics plus speeches by Aeschines and Demosthenes. Wide commentary marks the Horace and Lucretius editions, though he names his manuscripts less exactly than later scholars wish.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dolphin:
The dolphin served early Christians as a symbol tied to the wider use of the fish. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry explains that its swiftness pictures the eagerness with which Christians, sharers in Christ the true Fish, should seek knowledge of him. Pairs of dolphins are thus shown turning toward the sacred monogram or another emblem of Christ. In other cases the idea is love and tenderness.

Aringhi prints a dolphin with a heart, and other stones bear the motto thou hast a pledge of love. On tombs the dolphin can mark simple married love, while with an anchor it pictures the Christian clinging to Christ crucified. The entry thus reads a small sea creature as a sign of the single believer rather than of Christ himself.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-domingo-san-a:
Domingo Chimalpain was a Mexican Indian scholar of the late sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries. He was schooled in the colleges for Indians at Mexico City under clerical direction. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how his family, having gained some wealth, backed his study of the antiquities of his own people. He wrote several works in Spanish and Nahuatl on the Mexican past.

Bustamante printed one of his works as Gomara's chronicle, though it seems a copy or paraphrase of it. He is credited with an ancient Mexican history, a chronicle from 1068 to 1597, notes on events from 1064 to 1521, and relations of the kingdoms of Aculhuacan and Mexico. The entry cautions that the attribution of some works is not yet certain.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dominique-par:
Dominique Parrenin was a Jesuit missionary born at Russey near Besancon on 1 September 1665. He joined the order in 1685 and was sent to China in 1697, reaching Peking the next year. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how his wide knowledge and easy use of Chinese and Tatar-Manchu won the favor of the emperor Kangxi. Parrenin used that favor for religion and for science alike.

While feeding the emperor's curiosity about physics, medicine, and European history, he showed how Western science owed its rise to Christianity. Traveling with the court, he visited native Christians and won great persons to look kindly on the spread of the faith. He died at Peking in 1741, a courtier-priest of two worlds.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dublin:
Dublin is an archdiocese covering about sixty miles of Ireland's middle eastern coast and reaching some forty-six miles inland. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry gives its bounds as County Dublin whole, Wicklow nearly whole, and parts of Kildare and Wexford. Its suffragans are Kildare and Leighlin, Ferns, and Ossory. The whole spans nearly seven hundred thousand statute acres.

Ptolemy in the second century marked Eblana on his map at Dublin's latitude. The annals first name Duibhlinn, black pool, under the year 291, for a river where the king of Ireland fought the Leinstermen. The entry follows the see from those early notices through centuries of Irish church history, citing Shearman, Halliday, and the public records.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dunedin:
Dunedin is a diocese covering the Otago provincial district of New Zealand, with Southland, Stewart Island, and nearby isles. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry praises its lake and fiord scenery, the most picturesque in the country. Its area runs to about twenty-four thousand square miles, with four thousand of goldfields and more than two thousand of forest. Captain Cook may have visited this coast in 1770.

Beyond a few traders, no white settlers came until 1840, when families settled at Waikouaiti. In 1848 the Otago Association colonized the district on a large scale under the Free Church of Scotland, hoping to keep it a Free Kirk reserve. Catholic newcomers at first faced a cool welcome, and the entry traces how the diocese grew despite it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-durand-ursin:
Durand Ursin was a Benedictine of the Maurist congregation, born at Tours on 20 May 1682. He took vows at Marmoutier at nineteen and gave himself to diplomatics, the study of old charters. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how in April 1709 he joined his brother Edmond Martene on a literary tour of France, gathering matter for a new Gallia Christiana. Having searched over eight hundred abbeys and a hundred cathedrals, they came back in 1713 to Saint-Germain-des-Pres.

Their haul filled the Gallia Christiana in part, while the rest appeared as the New Treasury of Anecdotes in five folio volumes from 1717. In 1718 the two set out anew, and the entry follows Durand to his later years. Branded a Jansenist appellant, he was sent to Noyon, then allowed to retire to Paris, where he spent his last years in letters.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-durandus-of-s:
Durandus of Saint-Pourcain was a philosopher and theologian born at Saint-Pourcain in Auvergne. He died at Meaux on 13 September 1332. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how he joined the Dominicans at Clermont and took his doctorate at Paris in 1313. Summoned to Avignon by John the Twenty-Second, he became Master of the Sacred Palace, explaining Scripture there. In 1318 he became bishop of Le Puy, moving to Meaux in 1326.

He earned the name Most Resolute Doctor for his vigorous defense of views new to the schoolmen. His works include commentaries on the Sentences and treatises on jurisdiction and on souls after death. His nominalism ran so far against the realism of his day that scholars date the third age of scholasticism from him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edmund-cosin:
Edmund Cosin, also spelled Cosyn, was a Cambridge scholar whose birth and death dates are not known. Born in Bedfordshire, he entered King's Hall as a Bible clerk and took degrees in 1535, 1541, and 1547, holding fellowships at King's Hall, Saint Catharine's, and Trinity. Under Queen Mary he became Master of Saint Catharine's and chaplain to Bishop Bonner.

In 1558 he was chosen Vice-Chancellor of Cambridge, but as a Catholic he would not accept the Elizabethan church settlement. He gave up all his posts in 1560, lived in retirement at Caius College, and in 1568 chose exile over a forced oath. He was still living abroad in 1576, and the record then goes silent. The entry is a short, honest sketch of a career cut off by conscience.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edward-coffin:
Edward Coffin, also known as Hatton, was an English Jesuit missionary born at Exeter in 1570 and dead at Saint-Omer in 1626. After study at Reims and Ingolstadt he was ordained at the English College in Rome and sent to England. He entered the Society in 1598, but on his way to the novitiate in Flanders the Dutch seized him near Antwerp and took him to England.

There he spent five years in prison before banishment in 1603. For twenty years he served as confessor at the English College in Rome, and he died on the road while volunteering for England once more. His writings include a preface to Father Persons, a reply to Dean Hall, and an Art of Dying Well drawn from Bellarmine, plus a short life of Bellarmine in his last illness.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edward-sorin:
Edward Sorin founded the University of Notre Dame in Indiana, living from 1814 to 1893. Born at Ahuille near Laval in France, he was taught at first by his mother and then in the diocesan seminary, where he stood out for ability and good life. Drawn at first to China, he instead joined the Congregation of the Holy Cross, newly founded at Le Mans by Abbe Moreau.
