His skill with keys tempted him toward grand burglary, fine clothes, and showy women. Fear of capture held him to seductions and small, safe break-ins, leaving his ambition unsatisfied. He tormented weaker comrades, set stronger ones against each other, and had no friends. One tired evening walk begins to change the direction of his life.
the-romanization-of-roman-britain: F. Haverfield's study asks how Roman ways took hold in Britain. The Clarendon Press at Oxford issued it in 1912. That printing was a second edition, greatly enlarged. It carried twenty-one illustrations. Presented here are just the title page and contents. Haverfield's argument itself is absent. The contents promise chapters on Romanization across the empire. Later chapters treat Britain through language and material civilization. Others cover art, local government, and the land system. A chronology follows. The closing chapter turns to the Celtic revival in the later empire.
the-rulers-of-the-lakes-a-story-of-georg:
Joseph A. Altsheler's The Rulers of the Lakes was copyrighted in 1917. D. Appleton and Company held the copyright. The subtitle calls it a story of George and Champlain. A prefatory summary sets the tale in the French and Indian War. The time is just after Braddock's defeat. A character list names Robert Lennox and Tayoga. He is a young Onondaga warrior. The hunter David Willet and several French officers appear.

According to that summary, Lennox and Tayoga travel through the northern wilderness. Their errand is dangerous. They must warn Fort Refuge of hostile forces. The garrison and settlers there are in peril. Afterwards the pair join the army as scouts. They precede it toward Lake George and Lake Champlain. The story concludes with the battle of Lake George. The summary calls it the colonists' first great success of the war.
the-saddle-boys-of-the-rockies-or-lost-o: Captain James Carson published The Saddle Boys of the Rockies with Cupples and Leon in 1913. Its subtitle is Lost on Thunder Mountain. A frontispiece caption describes a big black horse acting as though it had gone wild. Preserved here are the title pages and the start of the contents only. The story itself is left out. Early chapters promise a challenge accepted and the strange actions of Domino. A note of warning waits at the spring hole.
the-second-violin: Grace S. Richmond wrote The Second Violin, published in New York by A. L. Burt Company. Richmond also wrote Red Pepper Burns and Mrs. Red Pepper, the title page notes. Copyrights of 1905 and 1906 are listed. The book was published in September 1906. The portion shown gives the title matter and contents only. Two books are listed, each with ten chapters. The first book shares the volume's title. The second is called The Churchill Latch-string. No chapter titles are given, and no story text appears.
the-spirit-of-the-border-a-romance-of-th:
Zane Grey published this romance of the early settlers in the Ohio Valley in 1906, dedicating it to his brother with memories of days in forest solitude. His introduction refuses to apologize for the story's wild spirit. He insists that its brutality is true to western border life. That life lay a little more than a hundred years in the past.

Grey says he holds papers of undoubted truth. Chief among them is a long-lost journal. His ancestor Colonel Ebenezer Zane kept it. Zane was a leading hunter and pioneer of the western settlement. From those notes he means to show the fever of freedom. It lured pioneers toward unmarked graves. He hopes their heroism and sacrifice will gain a higher place in history books.
the-story-of-porcelain: Sara Ware Bassett wrote this industrial story for young readers. Her companion volumes cover lumber, wool, leather, glass, sugar, and silk. The Penn Publishing Company of Philadelphia published this book in 1919. Isabel W. Caley illustrated it. Only the title pages are present here, with two short pieces. Bassett's inscription to Margaret Huxley is affectionate. The opening lines of a piece called The Bowl follow. A master-craftsman in it makes porcelain for the Emperor, the Son of Heaven. The story itself does not appear beyond its threshold.
the-tale-of-squirrel-nutkin:
Beatrix Potter's Squirrel Nutkin was published by Frederick Warne in 1903 as a story for Norah. Potter calls it a tale about a tail, the tail of a little red squirrel named Nutkin. He has a brother, Twinkleberry, and many cousins living in a wood beside a lake. On an island in the lake stands a hollow oak, home of an owl called Old Brown.

One autumn, when the nuts ripen, the squirrels paddle to the island on little rafts of twigs to gather food. Their visits to Old Brown's tree set the story in motion. Potter mixes real woodland habits with a cheeky hero who teases a dangerous neighbor, and young readers learn why Nutkin's tail matters.
the-treasure-train:
Arthur B. Reeve's Treasure-Train gathers Craig Kennedy detective stories, opening as Maude Euston visits Professor Kennedy in his laboratory. Maude begins by protesting she is no spy, though circumstances force her toward it. She is Barry Euston's striking, sincere daughter; he presides over the Continental railroad. Her problem is worthy of the scientific detective. The frontispiece is by Will Foster.

The contents promise Kennedy's arsenal of wonders: a truth-detector, soul-analysis, a mystic poisoner, a phantom destroyer, a love meter, a rubber dagger, a submarine mine, and sunken treasure. Reeve's Kennedy was America's answer to Sherlock Holmes by way of the laboratory. Readers who like detection done with instruments, wires, and chemistry will find each story built around a new scientific trick.
the-trial-or-more-links-of-the-daisy-cha: Charlotte M. Yonge's Trial is subtitled More Links of the Daisy Chain and dated 1864. It is present here as a title page and little more. A bare list of chapter numbers runs to twenty-nine, with no chapter titles and no text. The May family continues in this sequel, but nothing of their trial can be gathered from a column of numerals. Readers can confirm the book's identity and length, and that is all. A companion record of the same novel in this library does open with chapter one.
the-verse-of-alfred-lichtenstein:
Alfred Lichtenstein critiques his own verse in a short, dry self-assessment. Many readers, he begins, do not understand his poetry correctly or clearly. The first eighty poems are lyric in the usual sense, close to garden-praising verse about love's distress, death, and universal longing, though written in a cynical, cabaret-like vein.

Most of those eighty, he says flatly, are insignificant and were never shown to the public. One long night poem is quoted in full as the exception. Later poems fall into three groups, one mixing fantastic, half-playful images in pieces like The Sad Man and The Patent-Leather Shoe. Several first appeared in journals such as Aktion, Simplicissimus, and Pan.
the-world-s-great-sermons-volume-01-basi: Grenville Kleiser compiled The World's Great Sermons, and volume one runs from Basil to Calvin. Title pages and advertisements for Kleiser's speaking books are what appear here. Funk and Wagnalls published the ten-volume set in 1908. Lewis O. Brastow of Yale wrote the introduction. Kleiser had served on Yale Divinity School's faculty. Living preachers and theologians assisted the compilation. The sermons themselves begin beyond what is shown here.
the-wrong-twin:
Harry Leon Wilson's The Wrong Twin, dated 1921, opens its illustrations with a girl vowing to run away. Chapter one visits a photography shop in Newbern Center. Its window displays a portrait of Dave Cowan's twin sons. One twin sits forward with a bland, composed face. His brother scowls from behind and fights the camera. Even their curls show the difference between them.

Wilson builds comedy from two opposite temperaments in identical boys. Captions promise palm reading and a proudly worn black eye. Small-town characters fill out the scene. Readers can expect mistaken-identity humor with a warm heart. The twins' contrast powers every misunderstanding that follows.
the-young-captives-a-narrative-of-the-sh:
The Young Captives, dated 1850, narrates the shipwreck and sufferings of John and William Doyley. Their ship, the Charles Eaton, was wrecked in the Southern Ocean. A picture shows the crew escaping on a raft of spars. They reached an island shore exhausted and fell asleep. Islanders attacked the helpless castaways and killed nearly everyone. Captain, crew, and passengers all died in that attack.

The two Doyley boys alone were spared and kept captive. Their parents had been passengers on the doomed ship. The account retells a real and notorious shipwreck story. Victorian readers consumed such tales of danger eagerly. The boys' survival and rescue form the narrative's heart.
the-zincali-an-account-of-the-gypsies-of: George Borrow's The Zincali, an account of the Gypsies of Spain, appears here in a 1901 John Murray impression. Title pages name Borrow as author of The Bible in Spain and Lavengro. An epigraph from Ferdousi voices a harsh old prejudice about Gypsies. A dedication letter to the Earl of Clarendon begins at the end. The account itself does not appear within the pages present in this record.
time-and-time-again:
H. Beam Piper's story first appeared in Astounding Science Fiction in April 1947, illustrated by Napoli. Its opening note says upsetting time's mighty stream would take enormous energy, and no man expects a second chance at life. An atomic blast, it suggests, might accomplish both.

Captain Allan Hartley lies blinded by bomb flash and numbed by narcotics, knowing he is dying. Medics read his identity badge and recognise the author of Children of the Mist and Conqueror's Road. Another injection closes soft oblivion around his last spark of awareness. Readers get a time story that begins at death.
trailin: Max Brand published his western novel in 1919 and dedicated it to Robert Hobart Davis, called a maker of books and men. A contents list begins with a ringmaster's cry to ladies and gentlemen, then a sporting chance and social suicide. Anthony is left in the dark in chapter five. John Bard, Bluebeard's room, and Marty Wilkes follow, before a quest begins and a touch of crimson appears. A contents list alone is held in this record, so Brand's western itself is not shown.
trithemius-polygraphia-1518-latin:
Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, published his Polygraphia in 1518, the first printed book on cryptography. Six Latin books set out systems of secret writing in order. With this work, codes and ciphers became a systematic art that scholars could study rather than a bag of tricks.

Trithemius wrote for princes and prelates who needed letters no enemy could read. His tables and wheels turned plain words into ordered secrecy. The Polygraphia is the open companion to his darker Steganographia, which hid messages behind angels. Together they founded the literature of secret writing. Modern historians of codes begin their story with the abbot's six books.
trithemius-steganographia-latin:
Abbot Johannes Trithemius wrote the Steganographia, a book of secret writing, around 1500. It circulated in manuscript and was printed in Latin in 1608. Trithemius was a famed scholar of codes and monastic learning.

On the surface, the book teaches how to call spirits for messages. Inside, its lists and tables hide a true cipher system. Scholars long debated which face was real. The work earned its author a dark name for magic. It remains a Renaissance crypto classic, read by code historians and occultists alike for its double game. Its double face still draws new readers today.
un-doc-international-review-of-criminal-:
International Harmonization belongs to the privacy part of the United Nations manual printed in the International Review of Criminal Policy, Nos. 43 and 44. If each land guards data its own way, files snag at the border. Three Western bodies tried to line the rules up. Their work set the pattern most states still use.

The OECD's 1980 guides list eight ground rules, from tight limits on gathering to a duty to answer for misuse. The Council of Europe's 1980 pact binds its members to ten shared points. Europe's bloc drafted a common data law in 1990. The United Nations Assembly added its own file guides that same era. Crime law lags far behind. Experts urge it be used last, with sharp wording and proof of intent.
under-drake-s-flag-a-tale-of-the-spanish:
G. A. Henty's Under Drake's Flag, a tale of the Spanish Main, lists twenty-two chapters before the story starts. A wreck on the Devon coast, the Inquisition's prison, the Golden Hind, and San Francisco Bay mark the route. Chapter one opens on a stormy May morning in 1572.

Fishermen of Westport, five miles from Plymouth, crowd their public house to discuss Francis Drake's visit to the local squire. Every man there would gladly ship with Drake for the booty of the Spanish Main. Henty notes that fighting men, soldiers by trade, formed the strength of such crews. A Devon boy's path to Drake's fleet begins in that alehouse talk.
under-the-greenwood-tree-or-the-mellstoc: Thomas Hardy's Under the Greenwood Tree, subtitled The Mellstock Quire, survives here through its contents. The novel divides into four seasonal parts. Winter opens with the assembled quire going its Christmas rounds. Spring brings an interview with the vicar, summer a confession and an arrangement, and autumn closes with nutting, honey-taking, and second thoughts. Only the contents are present here, so the novel itself does not appear.
wake-robin:
John Burroughs called his first bird book Wake-Robin, and the preface to its first edition, kept at the front of volume one of his writings, states his aim. The book is mainly about the birds, or rather an invitation to the study of ornithology. Its purpose succeeds in the measure that it wakes and stirs the reader's interest in that branch of natural history.

Burroughs writes, he says, more with the freedom of love and old acquaintance than with exact science. Still, he pledges that he has taken no liberties with facts and let no fancy give a false color. His harvest was reaped more in the woods than in the study, and the pursuit, chase, and discovery of birds pleased him most. Readers get field notes from a man who carried birdsong with him in eye and ear wherever he went.
weller-die-falschen-und-fingirten-drucko: Die falschen und fingirten Druckorte, Repertorium, by Weller. The false imprints. This book preserves that repertory. It retains its place in time. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
where-the-sabots-clatter-again:
Katherine Shortall wrote the sketches in Where the Sabots Clatter Again after service in France. She drove for the Radcliffe Unit, which worked with the French Red Cross on rebuilding after the Armistice. Ralph Fletcher Seymour printed the book in Chicago in 1921 for the Radcliffe College fund. Her first sketch, The Bride of Noyon, opens in the summer of 1919.

Green blades and poppies spread over the old No Man's Land. Shell holes and trenches soften under new growth. Blue and white flowers follow the red ranks of poppies. Shortall finds hope in villages where wooden shoes clatter once more. War's waste and slow repair fill these short pieces.
william-tell-told-again: The front pages here hold a transcriber's note and the start of a picture list for William Tell Told Again, with P. G. Wodehouse's tale not yet begun. Wodehouse published the book in 1904. The note explains that two children's books sit in one cover. Philip Dadd's picture book, with verse by John W. Houghton, is one part. Wodehouse's comic novel, built on the pictures, is the other. In this text the verses move to the end. The book went to Biddy O'Sullivan as a Christmas gift.
with-methuen-s-column-on-an-ambulance-tr:
Ernest N. Bennett wrote With Methuen's Column on an Ambulance Train after service in South Africa. His preface says he had not meant to add to the flood of war books. A friend urged print as a way to raise money for Lady Lansdowne's fund for officers' widows and families. Bennett's share of the profits goes to that fund. Swan Sonnenschein printed the book in London in 1900.

The tale opens with a first view of Cape Town from the sea at sunrise. Light picks out houses between Table Mountain and the bay. Bennett rode with an ambulance train in Methuen's column during the Boer War. Care of the wounded, not combat, fills his pages. Charity and witness shape the book.
yet-again: Max Beerbohm gathered these essays from magazines and papers where they first appeared. His short opening note lists outlets from the Saturday Review to Harper's Magazine. Pages present here hold that note and a contents list, but no essay text. Listed pieces cover seeing people off, a club in ruins, Whistler's writing, and the humour of the public. One section promises words for pictures. The essays themselves do not appear in these pages.
you-ll-git-dar-in-de-mornin:
H. T. Burleigh set music to words by F. L. Stanton for this short song. Two verses appear in full here. Each verse urges the listener to keep going through hard luck. Keep looking for bright skies, keep hoping the sun will rise, and keep singing while the world sighs, the first verse says. The refrain promises arrival in the morning.

The second verse turns to farm and stage images. Keep ploughing after missed crops and dancing after the fiddle stops. Faithfulness until the curtain drops earns the same promise. Readers get a complete, hopeful song in dialect spelling, brief enough to read at a glance.
young-peoples-history-of-the-war-with-sp:
Prescott Holmes wrote this history of the Spanish-American War for young readers, copyrighted in 1900. Eighty-six pictures support the text. His introduction frames the war as an act of humanity. Americans sent food and medicine to starving Cubans, he writes. When Spain's cruelty grew intolerable, the United States stepped in and demanded an end to it. War followed Spain's resentment.

Holmes praises the navy's clean record without reserve. Army management, by contrast, drew grave scandal, he admits. Young readers get a patriotic account that still names faults at home. Cuba's suffering stays the stated cause throughout.
